title: Count the Number of Houses at a Certain Distance II
statement:
Houses are labelled `1` to `n`. Every pair of consecutive labels `i` and `i + 1` is joined by a street, and one more street joins house `x` to house `y` (`x` may equal `y`, in which case it adds nothing). The distance between two houses is the fewest streets you must walk to get from one to the other.

Return an array `result` of length `n` where `result[k - 1]` is the number of **ordered** pairs of different houses `(a, b)` whose distance is exactly `k`, for every `k` from `1` to `n`. Since pairs are ordered, `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` both count.
signature: long[] countOfPairs(int n, int x, int y)
notes:
## Intuition

A breadth-first search from every house gives all distances but costs O(n²). Instead, look at the shape of the map: with `x <= y`, houses `x..y` form a **cycle** of `cycle = y - x + 1` houses (the extra street closes it), houses `1..x-1` hang off `x` as a **left tail**, and houses `y+1..n` hang off `y` as a **right tail**. From any one house, the distances to each part are runs of consecutive numbers that can be written down directly. Adding "one pair at every distance from `lo` to `hi`" is a range update, so a difference array collects all of them in O(1) each.

On a cycle, the other houses sit on two arms going each way round: one arm reaches distances `1..floor(cycle/2)` and the other `1..floor((cycle-1)/2)`.

## Approach

1. Swap so `x <= y`. Set up `diff` and `addRange(lo, hi)`, which adds 1 to every distance in `[lo, hi]` (nothing if `lo > hi`).
2. `bridge` is the cost of the extra street between `x` and `y`: 1, or 0 when `x === y`.
3. For a tail house `i` at `t` steps from its attachment point: walking towards the cycle gives distances `1..t`; walking away gives `1..ownTail - t`; the two cycle arms give `t+1..t+floor(cycle/2)` and `t+1..t+floor((cycle-1)/2)`; the other tail starts after the bridge, at `t + bridge + 1`.
4. For a cycle house `i` at offset `p` from `x`: add the two arms, then each tail starting one step past the shortest way round to its attachment point (`toX` or `toY`).
5. Prefix-sum `diff` into `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3, x = 1, y = 3`: `cycle = 3` and both tails are empty. Each of the three houses is on the cycle and adds the arms `[1, 1]` and `[1, 1]`, so `diff[1] = 6` and `diff[2] = -6`. The prefix sums are `[6, 0, 0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each house makes at most five range updates, then one prefix-sum pass.
- Space: O(n) for `diff` and `result`.

## Pitfalls

- Pairs are ordered: every house counts its own view, so each unordered pair is counted twice, as required.
- When `x === y` the extra street costs nothing extra but also saves nothing; `bridge = 0` handles the tail-to-tail distance.
- A path between the tails always uses the extra street, because going round the cycle the long way is never shorter.
- Answers grow to about n², so in Java and C use 64-bit counts.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `diff` | difference array over distances |
| `addRange` | adds one pair to every distance in a range |
| `cycle` | number of houses from `x` to `y` |
| `bridge` | length of the extra street (0 if `x === y`) |
| `leftTail`, `rightTail` | sizes of the tails on each side |
| `t` | steps from a tail house to its attachment point |
| `ownTail`, `otherTail` | size of the tail containing `i`, and of the opposite tail |
| `p`, `toX`, `toY` | offset of a cycle house and its distances to `x` and `y` |
| `running` | prefix sum giving the count at distance `k` |
